Not to my knowledge. Every mid-to-high-end 3D printer I'm aware of will read this kind of code on its own, and can also plug into a computer that runs the printer remotely. The kind of printer that would accurately reproduce gun parts will probably have the option to handle the code on its own, right out of the box.

The same code has been used for many years now. Its really just short lines of simple numbers and letters that tell a machine where/when/how to move, so there's not a lot there that could be changed over time.

When/if you decide to buy one, just ask the seller if their printer will handle "plug-and-play with a Gcode text file on a USB stick." That will be enough for a yes/no answer.

And as other people have said, make sure the printer is big enough to print your parts before buying. The same way you'll never be able to print a 12"x12" paper picture out of a 8.5" slot, you'll never be able to print a 12"x12"x12" cube out of a 6"x6"x6" space.
